explain.say: Imagine a farm that moves! In rainforests from the Amazon to Borneo and north-east India, some families farm a patch for a few years, then move on and let the forest grow back. Look at the board. This circle is called shifting cultivation, or slash and burn.

explain.say: The old plot is left for 10 to 20 years, and the forest grows back as the soil recovers. Wonderful work! Think about this: it works well when few people share a big forest, but with more people, plots are reused too soon and the forest cannot recover.

faq.a: It is farming where a forest plot is cleared and farmed for a few years, then left to grow back while the farmer moves to a new plot. It is also called slash and burn or swidden farming.
asks: What is slash and burn farming?

faq.q: Why do farmers burn the plot?
faq.a: Burning clears the cut plants quickly, and the ash adds minerals that make the soil better for crops for a short time. It also kills weeds and pests.

faq.q: Why does the soil wear out so fast?
faq.a: Rainforest soil is thin, and most of its goodness comes from fallen leaves. Once the forest is cleared, heavy rain washes the minerals away, so after two or three years crops grow poorly.
asks: Why do harvests shrink after a few years?

faq.a: It can be, if each plot is left long enough, often 10 to 20 years or more, and few people share a large forest. When more people farm the same land, rest periods get shorter and the land is damaged.
asks: Is slash and burn bad for the forest?

faq.a: Jhum is the name for shifting cultivation in north-east India, in states like Nagaland, Mizoram and Meghalaya. Rice, maize, millet and vegetables are grown together on hillside plots.
asks: Where is shifting cultivation practised in India?

facts: Shifting cultivation is called jhum in north-east India.
Traditionally, plots in shifting cultivation were left to regrow for 10 to 20 years or more.
Shifting cultivation is still practised in parts of the Amazon, Central Africa, South-east Asia and north-east India.
